content_html:
Two loan offers can look similar and still cost very different amounts. One may have a lower rate but a fee, another a lower payment but a longer term. This loan comparison calculator puts up to three fixed-rate offers side by side and shows the monthly payment, total interest, fees, total cost of borrowing and an APR that includes the fees, so you can see which deal is really cheaper.

How to use this calculator

  1. Loan amount: how much you would borrow under each offer. Keep it the same for a like-for-like comparison.
  2. Interest rate: the rate quoted for each loan.
  3. Term: the length of each loan in years. Half years such as 2.5 are fine.
  4. Upfront fees: origination, application, documentation or closing fees. Include fees that are taken out of the loan proceeds, because they reduce the cash you actually receive.
  5. Untick Include loan C if you only have two offers.

How the comparison works

For each loan the calculator works out the standard amortized monthly payment, L × i ÷ (1 − (1 + i)−n), where L is the loan amount, i the annual rate divided by 12 and n the number of monthly payments. Total interest is all the payments minus the amount borrowed, and the total cost of borrowing adds the upfront fees on top.

The APR including fees answers a different question: what interest rate would make the payments worth exactly the cash you receive after fees? Because there is no direct formula for that, the calculator finds it by trial and error to a fraction of a basis point. A loan with no fees has an APR equal to its interest rate; a fee pushes the APR above the rate, and the shorter the loan, the bigger the push.

Worked example

Three offers for $25,000:

OfferMonthly paymentTotal cost of borrowingAPR
A: 7.5%, 3 years, no fee$777.66$2,995.607.500%
B: 6.9%, 5 years, $500 fee$493.85$5,131.087.750%
C: 8.9%, 7 years, no fee$400.96$8,680.598.900%

Loan B advertises the lowest rate, yet its $500 fee lifts its APR above loan A's. Loan C has the smallest payment but costs $5,684.99 more than loan A over its life, mostly because interest runs for seven years instead of three.

Choosing between offers

  • Lowest total cost is the right yardstick if you can comfortably afford the payment on every option.
  • Lowest payment matters when monthly cash flow is tight, but you usually pay for it with a longer term and more interest.
  • APR is the fairest single number when amounts or fees differ, and it is the figure lenders must disclose under the federal Truth in Lending Act.
  • If you expect to repay early, a loan with a large upfront fee loses its appeal, because you pay the whole fee but save only part of the interest.
  • Check for prepayment penalties, rate discounts for automatic payments and whether any fees are refundable.

faq.question: Is the loan with the lowest interest rate always the cheapest?
faq.answer: No. Upfront fees and the length of the loan both change the total cost. A slightly higher rate with no fee, or a shorter term, can cost less overall than a lower advertised rate.

faq.question: Why is the APR higher than the interest rate?
faq.answer: The APR treats fees as part of the cost of borrowing. Because you receive less cash than the amount you repay interest on, the effective rate you pay is higher than the stated rate.

faq.question: Should I pick a longer term to get a lower payment?
faq.answer: A longer term lowers the payment but usually raises total interest, sometimes by thousands of dollars. Many borrowers choose the longer term for flexibility and then pay extra when they can, as long as the loan has no prepayment penalty.

faq.question: Can I compare loans of different amounts?
faq.answer: Yes. The calculator shows each loan's totals separately. Dollar totals favor the smaller loan, so look at the APR as well when the amounts differ.

faq.question: Does this work for mortgages, car loans and personal loans?
faq.answer: It works for any fixed-rate loan with equal monthly payments. It does not model variable rates, balloon payments, mortgage insurance or property taxes.
